questions.prompt: Which beginning-of-construction method should the buyer rely on for Cottonwood Solar I?
questions.context: Seller relies on off-site physical manufacture of the custom transformer starting December 22, 2025 under a December 10, 2025 binding contract. The IE confirms on-site physical work only from January 12, 2026 and has not reviewed the off-site evidence. The December 18, 2025 NTP is not physical work. The answer sets the domestic content threshold (45% vs 50% against a computed 47.8%) and whether FEOC material assistance rules apply.

evidence.text: Physical manufacture of the transformer, beginning with cutting and stacking of the custom core, commenced at our facility on December 22, 2025 and continued thereafter.
On-site physical work of a significant nature, beginning with pile installation for the tracker foundations, commenced on January 12, 2026.
We have not reviewed the manufacturer's records and express no opinion on the tax treatment of off-site work.
If construction is determined to have begun in 2026, the applicable threshold would be 50% and the Project would not qualify at the computed adjusted percentage.
The sponsor's position is that the material assistance restrictions do not apply because construction began in 2025; certifications are provided for information.

options.label: Accept off-site transformer work: construction began December 22, 2025
options.consequence: The 45% domestic content threshold applies and 47.8% qualifies. FEOC material assistance rules do not apply. Buyer should still obtain the counsel memo, manufacturer records and IE review, and seek specific indemnity or insurance for the construction-start position.

options.label: Rely on on-site physical work: construction began January 12, 2026
options.consequence: The 50% domestic content threshold applies and 47.8% fails, which drops the credit rate to 40%. FEOC rules apply, and compliance cannot be shown until the module certification and MACR are delivered. Reprice or renegotiate.

options.label: Defer until Seller delivers the construction-start memo and manufacturer records reviewed by the IE
options.consequence: Construction start, domestic content and FEOC remain open. Make delivery a condition precedent before signing.

questions.prompt: How should the buyer treat the unpaid apprenticeship labor-hour cure?
questions.context: Apprentice hours are 13.2% against the 15.0% requirement, with no Good Faith Effort exception documented. Seller intends to pay the $370,800 penalty before placed in service, but it was unpaid as of September 22, 2026. Known PWA deficiencies are excluded from the insurance coverage.

evidence.text: The labor hour requirement is not satisfied for the period reviewed. The Seller has not documented a Good Faith Effort exception for the shortfall.
At $50 per labor hour, the cure payment would be $370,800. As of the report date, the payment has not been made
the client will make the cure payment before placed-in-service. We do not expect this to affect the credit.
Known prevailing wage or apprenticeship deficiencies as of binding; changes in law

options.label: Treat PWA as unmet until proof of the cure payment (on final hours) is delivered; make it a condition precedent
options.consequence: PWA stays unmet in the model until payment is evidenced. Closing waits on proof of payment and a final PWA report.

options.label: Accept Seller's covenant to cure before placed in service, backed by a specific indemnity
options.consequence: Keeps the 30% base rate assumption. Because the exposure is uninsured, Buyer relies on Seller/Sponsor credit for the full PWA-dependent credit value.

options.label: Assume PWA fails and reprice at the non-PWA credit rate
options.consequence: The base rate and bonuses drop to non-PWA levels, sharply reducing the credit amount and purchase price.
